questions.prompt: In the CIA triad of data security, what does "Confidentiality" mean?
options: Only people who are authorized to see the data can see it
The data is accurate and hasn't been tampered with, by an attacker, a bug, or an honest mistake
The data is accessible to legitimate users whenever they legitimately need it
The organization has documented a legal basis before collecting the data
The data was collected with the individual's informed, freely given consent
The data cannot be traced back to the specific system that produced it
questions.explain: Confidentiality is the CIA triad property that only authorized people can see the data — enforced through encryption, access controls, and authentication.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Integrity, not Confidentiality — Integrity is about the data being accurate and untampered, a different property of the CIA triad entirely. Confidentiality is specifically about who is allowed to see the data, not whether the data itself is correct.

questions.prompt: A company publishes a dataset with names and Social Security numbers removed, but every row still carries a 5-digit ZIP code, a full date of birth, and a gender. Based on Latanya Sweeney's re-identification research, what should the company conclude about this dataset?
options: It can very likely still be re-identified down to a specific individual, because that combination of three quasi-identifiers uniquely identifies most of the U.S. population
It is safely anonymized, since no direct identifier like a name or SSN remains
It would only be re-identifiable if the organization also published income data
Quasi-identifiers only become a re-identification risk when combined with at least five separate fields
questions.explain: Sweeney's 2000 study found that ZIP code, full date of birth, and gender together uniquely identify a large majority of the U.S. population — stripping only the direct identifiers (name, SSN) and leaving those three quasi-identifiers intact does not actually anonymize the data.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to whether the leaked data would be sensitive, confidential, both, or neither, per this course's definitions.
left: A customer's health record is leaked publicly
A company's unreleased merger plan is leaked to a competitor
An executive's salary and health benefits file is leaked
A company's already-published press release is leaked early
right: Both sensitive and confidential
Neither sensitive nor confidential
Sensitive only — harms the individual, not a business trade secret
Confidential only — harms the business, not any individual's health or biometrics
questions.explain: A health record is sensitive (personal harm) but not a business trade secret. An unreleased merger plan is confidential (business harm) but doesn't expose anyone's health or biometrics. An executive's salary-and-health file is both — personal harm to the executive and business harm from compensation data going public. A press release that's already meant for the public is neither — it was never sensitive or confidential in the first place.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Under GDPR, an organization must notify its supervisory authority of a personal-data breach without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than ________ hours after becoming aware of it.
questions.explain: GDPR sets a 72-hour notification expectation for informing the supervisory authority of a qualifying personal-data breach where feasible — one of the most frequently cited specific numbers in the regulation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the difference between GDPR's consent model and CCPA's consent model.
options: GDPR is opt-in — an organization needs an affirmative legal basis before processing personal data
CCPA is opt-out — collection and sale of personal information is allowed by default until the consumer acts to stop it
Both GDPR and CCPA use the same opt-in default, just enforced by different regulators
Under CCPA, a consumer has the right to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information
GDPR's consent standard requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous
questions.explain: GDPR defaults to 'no' — processing requires an affirmative legal basis such as strict, specific consent. CCPA defaults to 'yes' — collection and sale are allowed unless the consumer actively opts out, though CCPA does grant that opt-out right. The two regulations share the broad goal of giving people control over their data, but they are built on opposite defaults, not the same one.

questions.prompt: An organization decides to apply its strictest encryption, access control, and retention rules uniformly to every dataset it holds, including its public marketing spreadsheets. What's the main problem with this approach, per this course's classification concepts?
options: It wastes money and slows down work on data that was never risky, while not actually improving protection of the genuinely sensitive data
It's the recommended approach, since more security is always better regardless of cost
It violates GDPR, which requires every organization to classify data into at least four tiers
It eliminates the need for access reviews, since every dataset already has maximum controls
questions.explain: Classification exists specifically to avoid this failure mode: applying the highest-cost controls to everything is safe in isolation but enormously expensive and slow, and it doesn't right-size protection — the genuinely sensitive data doesn't get any more protected than the harmless marketing spreadsheet sitting next to it under the same blanket policy.

questions.prompt: Match each classification tier to the kind of data it's typically used for in the common four-tier commercial scheme.
right: Social Security numbers and health records
Published pricing and press releases
Customer records and pre-announcement financial results
An internal org chart or meeting agenda
questions.explain: Public data (press releases, published pricing) is fine for anyone to see. Internal data (an org chart, a meeting agenda) is meant for employees but not damaging if it leaked. Confidential data (customer records, pre-announcement financials) would cause real harm if disclosed. Restricted data (SSNs, health records) is the most sensitive tier, where a leak causes severe harm.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is Amazon's purpose-built service for discovering sensitive data stored in S3.
questions.explain: AWS Macie is the named example this course gives for Amazon's sensitive-data discovery service, alongside Microsoft Purview and Google Cloud DLP as the other two real platforms named.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the three general approaches to data discovery tooling.
options: Pattern/regex-based scanning checks whether a field's actual content matches the shape of sensitive data, regardless of what the column is named
Keyword/metadata-based discovery flags likely sensitive fields based on column or file names, without necessarily inspecting every row's content
Sampling-based scanning checks every single row in a dataset rather than a representative subset
Mature discovery tooling typically combines metadata scanning, pattern matching, and sampling rather than relying on just one
Keyword/metadata-based discovery is immune to missing sensitive data stored under a generic or unhelpful column name
questions.explain: Pattern/regex scanning looks at actual content shape; keyword/metadata scanning looks at names without necessarily reading content; sampling estimates from a representative subset rather than scanning every row — so the claim that sampling checks every row inverts what it actually does. Keyword/metadata scanning is specifically the approach that misses sensitive data sitting under a generically-named column, which is why mature tooling combines all three approaches rather than relying on just one.

questions.prompt: In the Joiner-Mover-Leaver lifecycle, why is the "Mover" event the one most likely to leave stale access behind?
options: Granting new access when someone changes roles has an obvious trigger — the new manager asks for it — but removing the old role's access has no equivalent automatic trigger unless the governance program creates one
Movers are not covered by access governance programs at all
SQL Server automatically revokes a user's old role membership the moment they join a new team
Movers always receive less access than Joiners, so there's nothing meaningful to remove
questions.explain: A Joiner's access and a Leaver's revocation both have a clear trigger (a start date, an end date). A Mover's new access also has a clear trigger (the new manager's request) — but removing the old access is nobody's job unless the governance program explicitly makes it one, which is exactly why permission creep accumulates through Mover events specifically.

questions.prompt: Put these four roles from an access-governance decision in the order they actually occur, from the original request through to the independent after-the-fact check.
items: Requester identifies a business need and submits the access request
Approver — typically the data or system owner — reviews and decides whether to approve it
Provisioner actually executes the grant in the target system
Auditor later confirms the grant was approved correctly and is still needed
questions.explain: Access governance runs requester to approver to provisioner to auditor: someone identifies a need and asks, an accountable owner decides whether it's justified, someone (or an automated workflow) actually executes the grant, and an independent auditor later confirms the grant was correct and is still appropriate — with no single person filling more than one of these roles for their own request.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of the three T-SQL permission statements GRANT, REVOKE, and DENY, a ________ on a column or table always wins, even if the same user also belongs to a role that GRANTs the identical permission.
questions.explain: DENY explicitly blocks a permission, and a DENY always overrides a GRANT for the same user — even if that GRANT comes from a different role the user also belongs to. REVOKE, by contrast, just returns to a neutral 'no explicit permission' state rather than actively blocking anything.

questions.prompt: Match each T-SQL permission statement to what it actually does.
right: Removes a previously granted permission, returning to a neutral state
Gives a permission
Explicitly blocks a permission, and always wins even over a GRANT from another role
questions.explain: GRANT gives a permission. REVOKE removes a previously granted permission, returning to a neutral 'no explicit permission' state. DENY explicitly blocks a permission and always wins, even if the same user holds a GRANT for that same permission through a different role.

questions.prompt: A service account was granted broad database access five years ago "just in case it's ever needed" for a migration that finished within a month. The account still holds that access today, unused. Why does this violate least privilege even though the access has never actually been misused?
options: Because least privilege is violated the moment access exceeds what a specific, current task requires — misuse isn't the test; unjustified access itself is the risk, since it enlarges the blast radius if that account is ever compromised
It doesn't violate least privilege, since no harm has actually occurred yet
It only becomes a least-privilege violation once an attacker actually uses the account
Least privilege only applies to human user accounts, not service accounts
questions.explain: Least privilege asks whether a specific task justifies a permission — not whether the permission has been misused yet. An account holding access it can no longer justify is a bigger target the moment it's compromised, which is exactly the blast-radius risk least privilege exists to shrink, regardless of whether anything bad has happened so far.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about segregation of duties (SoD), based on the accounts-payable example from this course.
options: SoD is about splitting a sensitive process across multiple people, not just restricting any one permission
If the same person can create a vendor, approve it, and issue payment, fraud now requires no collusion at all
A toxic combination is a specific pair of permissions or functions that should never be held by the same person
SoD is unnecessary as long as each individual permission involved is independently justified
An SoD conflict matrix lists sensitive functions and flags which pairs are toxic when combined
questions.explain: SoD splits a process, not a single permission — even when every individual permission is justified, letting one person hold all of them removes the independent check that would otherwise catch a mistake or stop fraud. If one person can create, approve, and pay a vendor alone, committing fraud requires no collusion at all, which is exactly the risk SoD exists to close. A conflict matrix is the tool that names these toxic pairs so they can be checked against before access is granted.

questions.prompt: An organization's PAM system is temporarily unreachable during an outage, and an administrator needs emergency access to restore a critical service. What is this scenario specifically describing the need for?
options: A break-glass account — a last-resort credential kept outside normal day-to-day access, tightly monitored, with every use triggering an alert and a mandatory after-the-fact review
A standard just-in-time elevation request through the normal PAM workflow
Permanently granting every administrator sysadmin rights so an outage never blocks access
Disabling session recording so the administrator can work faster during the outage
questions.explain: A break-glass account exists precisely for the scenario where the normal privileged-access system itself is unavailable. It isn't the normal JIT elevation path (which depends on the PAM system being up), and it's tightly controlled and monitored — used rarely, with every use triggering an automatic alert and review — specifically because it bypasses the organization's normal controls.

questions.prompt: What is tokenization, as distinct from encryption?
options: Replacing a sensitive value with a substitute token that has no mathematical relationship to the original, reversible only by looking it up in a separate token vault
Mathematically transforming a value so it can be reversed back to plaintext by anyone holding the right key
Replacing a value with a type-appropriate placeholder like XXXX or 0, with no way to recover the original value at all
Hiding a value from a specific query result without changing what's physically stored on disk
Removing the ability to re-identify a person from a dataset entirely, with no mapping to reverse
Scoping a GRANT statement to a specific column instead of an entire table
questions.explain: Tokenization swaps a sensitive value for a token with no mathematical relationship to the original — the only way back to the real value is a lookup in a tightly controlled token vault, not a computation.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes encryption, not tokenization. An encrypted value is mathematically reversible with the right key — the ciphertext itself still encodes the original data — while a token is an arbitrary reference that means nothing without the vault's lookup table; there's no computation that gets you from a token back to the original value.

questions.prompt: A table's SSN column has Dynamic Data Masking applied with partial(1,"XXX-XX-",4). A support rep without the UNMASK permission runs SELECT SSN FROM dbo.Customers. What should they see, and why is this control described as limited against a determined attacker?
options: They see the masked value, not the real SSN — but masking is a presentation-layer control, so a user with enough query access can sometimes infer the real value indirectly, which is why it's not a substitute for encryption and tight permissioning
They see the fully real SSN, because masking only applies to INSERT and UPDATE statements, not SELECT
The query fails with a permissions error, because masked columns can't be selected at all
They see the real SSN only once, then the mask is permanently removed for that column
questions.explain: Dynamic Data Masking changes what a SELECT returns, not what's stored — a non-privileged user sees the masked value. But because the underlying data and its real distribution are still queryable indirectly, a sufficiently permissioned or determined user can sometimes infer masked values through clever queries, which is exactly why Microsoft's own documentation describes it as limiting casual, accidental exposure rather than acting as a real security boundary.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Always Encrypted moves encryption and decryption to the ________, outside the database engine entirely, so that even a sysadmin querying the column directly sees only ciphertext.
questions.explain: Always Encrypted performs encryption and decryption in the client driver rather than inside the database engine, which is what lets it protect data even from a database administrator with sysadmin rights — a guarantee that TDE and cell-level encryption, which both decrypt inside the engine, don't provide.

questions.prompt: Match each SQL Server Dynamic Data Masking function to what it does.
right: Replaces a numeric value with a random number within a specified range
Masks an address to a fixed pattern like aXXX@XXXX.com while keeping it recognizably shaped
Replaces the value with a type-appropriate placeholder such as XXXX or 0
Keeps a specified number of characters at the start and end, replacing the middle
questions.explain: default() substitutes a generic type-appropriate placeholder. partial() keeps a defined prefix and suffix while masking the middle, as with an SSN mask. email() keeps a value recognizably email-shaped while hiding the real address. random() swaps a numeric value for a random number in a range, useful where only the rough existence of a value matters, not its exact figure.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about tokenization, pseudonymization, and anonymization.
options: A token has no mathematical relationship to the original value — it can only be reversed through a vault lookup
Pseudonymized data is still considered personal data under GDPR, because it remains reversible via a mapping table
Anonymized data generally falls outside regulations like GDPR because there is no mapping left to reverse
Pseudonymization and anonymization are the same technique under two different names
A tokenization scheme with an unsecured token vault still provides meaningful protection, since the tokens themselves are safe to expose
questions.explain: Tokens are irreversible by computation, only by vault lookup. Pseudonymized data stays personal data under GDPR precisely because a mapping can reverse it, while truly anonymized data has no mapping to reverse and generally falls outside the regulation. Pseudonymization and anonymization are explicitly distinct — one is reversible by design, the other isn't. And an unsecured vault or mapping table provides no real protection at all; it just relocates the sensitive data to a second place that now also needs defending.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of setting up Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) in SQL Server in the correct order.
items: Create a master key in the master database, protected by a password
Create a certificate, protected by the master key
Create a database encryption key, protected by the certificate
Turn encryption on for the database with ALTER DATABASE ... SET ENCRYPTION ON
questions.explain: TDE's setup follows a chain where each layer protects the one below it: the master key protects the certificate, the certificate protects the database encryption key, and only after that key exists does turning ALTER DATABASE ... SET ENCRYPTION ON actually start encrypting the database's data and log files.

questions.prompt: A finance team deletes seven-year-old invoices after only one year to "keep things clean," while a separate customer-records table has sat completely unused for eight years and was never reviewed for deletion. What does this course call each of these two mistakes?
options: The invoice deletion is under-retention (deleted before a legal obligation expired); the unused customer records are over-retention (kept with no legitimate need, increasing breach exposure)
Both are examples of the same mistake: over-retention
Both are examples of the same mistake: under-retention
Neither is a retention problem, since retention schedules only apply to financial records
questions.explain: Under-retention deletes data before a legal, tax, or contractual obligation to keep it has expired — purging invoices after one year when a rule requires seven creates an audit finding. Over-retention keeps data long after any legitimate need, which is its own liability: every extra year of unused customer records is another year of breach exposure and another year someone eventually has to honor an erasure request against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: GDPR's "right to erasure," commonly called the right to be forgotten, is granted under Article ________.
questions.explain: GDPR Article 17 grants individuals a conditional right to request deletion of their personal data, subject to specific exceptions such as a legal obligation requiring continued retention.

questions.prompt: Match each data subject right to what it actually grants the individual.
right: Deletion of personal data, under specific conditions
Correcting inaccurate or incomplete data
A copy of the personal data an organization holds about them
Receiving their data in a structured, commonly-used format to move to another provider
questions.explain: Access grants a copy of the data held about the individual. Rectification corrects inaccurate or incomplete data. Erasure grants conditional deletion, covered in full in Lesson 24. Portability grants receiving the data in a structured, machine-readable format to move to another provider — a genuinely different output than a plain access request.

questions.prompt: An organization marks a customer's account row as deleted in its production database to fulfill an erasure request. Select every place this course names where a copy of that customer's data most likely still exists.
options: A nightly backup taken before the deletion
A search index or CDN cache that was never told the source row changed
An application log line that captured the customer's email address
A third-party email marketing platform the data was shared with
Nowhere — marking a row deleted in production removes it from every system it ever touched
questions.explain: Marking a row deleted in the production database is the easy part of an erasure request. Backups taken before the deletion still hold the data, caches and search indexes don't update just because the source row did, logs that captured personal data in a log line aren't touched by deleting the account, and any third-party processor the data was shared with needs its own separate deletion request. A credible erasure process has to name all of these up front, not discover them one at a time.

questions.prompt: Put these five stages of the breach response lifecycle in the order this course teaches them.
items: Detect — something triggers the alarm, such as a monitoring alert or an unusual access pattern
Contain — stop the ongoing exposure before it's fully understood
Assess — determine what data was involved and how serious the impact is
Notify — inform the regulator and, where required, affected individuals
Remediate and review — fix the underlying cause and document what the incident revealed
questions.explain: The lifecycle runs detect, contain, assess, notify, remediate and review — and containment deliberately comes before full assessment, accepting an imperfect early picture in exchange for stopping an ongoing exposure immediately rather than waiting until everything is understood.

questions.prompt: In the Brightfield Retail case study, select every control gap this course identifies as having contributed to the incident.
options: The customer_orders table had never been run through a classification process
Access was granted by copying another team's permissions instead of scoping to the dashboard's actual needs
There was no access review or recertification process that would have caught the still-active login after the contract ended
The contractor's single login was compromised by an external attacker
Row-level security or masking could have reduced the exposure even with broad access granted
questions.explain: Brightfield's incident traced to a classification gap (the table was never classified), an access-control gap (role-copying instead of least privilege, with no recertification catching the stale login), and a missed opportunity in data protection (masking or row-level security would have shrunk the exposure even with broad access granted). The incident was never about an external attacker compromising a credential — it was an internal offboarding gap that let an already-granted login stay active for months after it should have been revoked.

questions.prompt: Of the five building blocks of an access governance model (role definitions, least-privilege mapping, segregation-of-duties rules, a request-and-approval workflow, and periodic recertification), which two does this course identify as the specific pieces missing from the Brightfield case study?
options: A request-and-approval workflow requiring a named, scoped justification, and a periodic recertification cadence that would have caught the still-active login
Role definitions and least-privilege mapping, since Brightfield had never defined any roles at all
Segregation-of-duties rules and role definitions, since the contractor held two conflicting roles
Least-privilege mapping and recertification, since Brightfield's roles were defined but never scoped narrowly enough
questions.explain: This course identifies the missing request-and-approval workflow (the contractor's access was granted on an informal 'give them what the analytics team has' ask, with no named justification or independent approver) and the missing recertification cadence (nothing ever reviewed whether the grant was still needed) as the two specific building blocks that would have caught this incident — a role-based model alone, even if role definitions existed, wouldn't have been enough on its own.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: under GDPR Article 35, a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is specifically required when processing is likely to result in a ________ risk to individuals.
questions.explain: GDPR Article 35 requires a DPIA specifically when processing is 'likely to result in a high risk' to individuals — the regulation calls out large-scale processing of sensitive data and systematic monitoring as examples that typically meet that bar.

questions.prompt: A Confidential customer table is joined with an Internal marketing table to produce a new combined dataset for a campaign analysis. No one manually relabels the result. What classification should the combined dataset actually carry, and why?
options: Confidential, because a dataset formed by joining sources inherits the highest classification among its inputs — the join itself doesn't reduce sensitivity just because one input was less sensitive
Internal, because averaging the two classifications rounds down to the lower tier
Public, because combining two internal datasets creates new information not covered by either original classification
The combined dataset has no classification until a steward manually assigns one from scratch, unrelated to either source's label
questions.explain: The inheritance rule is that a joined or merged dataset takes on the highest classification among its sources — here, Confidential — regardless of whether anyone remembers to manually relabel it. This is exactly the kind of propagation failure that classification governance exists to catch.

questions.prompt: Match each classification governance role to what it actually owns.
right: Implements the technical controls (encryption, access restriction, logging) a classification level requires
Decides what classification a specific dataset should carry, as the accountable business-side role
Owns the classification scheme itself — tier definitions, label names, and dispute resolution
Applies and maintains the classification label on a dataset in practice
questions.explain: The data owner decides the classification as the accountable business role. The data steward applies and maintains the label day to day. The data custodian implements the technical controls a label requires once applied. The governance committee owns the scheme itself — the tier definitions and the rules everyone else follows.
